judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on House Bill 123. It would have made it a crime for a health care provider to knowingly destroy, change, or falsify a patient's medical record. The penalty was higher when the goal was to hide a medical error, or abuse or neglect, that badly hurt or killed a patient. Paying someone to change or destroy a record would also be a crime. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The House voted 88-24. The Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on House Bill 261. It would have raised the punishment for a crime committed with other people to help gang activity. That part covered any defendant. A smaller part raised the punishment for someone with an earlier federal conviction for returning to the country illegally after being removed. Prosecutors would have had to prove these facts to a jury. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The House voted 84-29. The Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on House Bill 38. It would have barred credit card networks from using a special code that marks a store as a gun seller, and from keeping lists of North Carolina gun owners. Banks and credit unions were not covered. The attorney general could fine a network up to $5,000 for each violation, and people could sue for $10,000 for each one. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The House voted 77-38. The Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on House Bill 519. It would have cut back the care a minor can agree to alone. That list now covers pregnancy, some diseases, drug or alcohol treatment, and mental health care. The bill would have kept only pregnancy care, with a narrow exception for minors 16 and older. It also would have let parents see their child's medical records. There were four exceptions, such as when a parent is under investigation for a crime against the child. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The House voted 68-41. The Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on House Bill 606. It would have given people more time to sue over care that helped them change gender, with a deadline of 10 years after they turn 18. Claims that were already too old to file would have been revived. It also would have barred state money from paying for gender transition care for people in state prisons. An amendment kept state money available to treat urgent problems caused by earlier care. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The House voted 69-41. The Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on House Bill 636. It would have required every public school system to set up a committee of five parents and five staff to review library and classroom materials. Material showing sexual activity, or that is very vulgar, could not be called age appropriate. Any county resident could object to an item, and could sue the school system for $5,000 for each violation. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The House voted 63-46. The Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on House Bill 690. It would have cut off state-funded benefits, public housing help, and unemployment pay for people in the country without legal permission. Agencies would have had to check status first. Food aid was left out. Colleges would have had to check status when deciding in-state tuition and aid. Each duty applied only as far as federal law allows. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The House voted 68-43. The Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on House Bill 781. It would have barred a city or county from letting people camp or sleep overnight on public land. A local board could set aside one site for up to a year, but only if the state certified that it met rules for safety, sanitation and health services. Any resident or business owner could sue the local government to enforce the ban. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The House voted 69-42. The Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on House Bill 859. It would have barred cities and counties from running a guaranteed income program, which pays people regular cash they can spend on anything. Programs that require the person to work, look for work, or attend training were not covered. The legislature could still allow a program by passing a law. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The House voted 69-40. The Senate never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on House Bill 936. It would have rewritten the state's phone sales law around robocalls, meaning recorded, computer-made, or AI voice calls, and spam texts. Callers would need written permission first. Faking caller ID to cheat someone, or posing as a government official, would be banned. Charities, political calls and pollsters stayed exempt. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The Senate voted 32-15. The House refused the Senate's version and the bill died in a conference committee, so it did not become law.

A no vote was against it. The Senate voted 32-15. The House refused the Senate's version and the bill died in a conference committee, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on Senate Bill 1057. Proxy advisers are firms that tell large investors how to vote their shares at company meetings. An adviser who told clients to vote against a company's management would have had to say whether the advice rested on a written financial study, and to tell the company's board. Advisers would also register with the state, and could be sued. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The Senate voted 29-13. The House never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on Senate Bill 1082. It would have asked voters to add a right to work rule to the state constitution. The rule says a person cannot be denied a job for joining or not joining a labor union. North Carolina already has this in state law. Putting it in the constitution would make it harder for a future legislature to undo. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The Senate voted 30-16 to put the question on the November 2026 ballot. The House never voted on it, so the question did not go to voters.

The House never voted on it, so the question did not go to voters.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on Senate Bill 261. It would have dropped the state's 2030 goal of cutting power plant carbon dioxide by 70 percent, while keeping the 2050 goal of net zero. It also would have let electric utilities start charging customers for a large power plant while it is still being built, instead of waiting until it is finished. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The Senate voted 31-12. The House never voted on it, so it did not become law.

The Senate voted 31-12. The House never voted on it, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on Senate Bill 378. It would have ordered the state health department to drop Planned Parenthood as a Medicaid provider and end its Medicaid contracts. The department would have had to line up other providers for the same services. Despite the bill's name, that was the whole of what the House voted on. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The House voted 61-47. The Senate refused to take up the bill the next day, so it did not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on Senate Bill 554. It would have barred state-chartered banks and credit unions from refusing or ending service to a farmer because of the farm's greenhouse gas emissions or its use of fossil fuels. The state banking commissioner would check for this during routine exams. National banks were not covered, and the bill created no right to sue. A yes vote helped the bill move ahead. The Senate voted 36-11. The House never voted on it, so it did not become law.
